story.title: Sri Lanka Court Convicts 15 for 2019 Easter Sunday Bombings
story.summary: A Sri Lankan court has convicted 15 individuals for their involvement in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings that targeted three churches and three luxury hotels, resulting in the deaths of 279 people. The attacks were inspired by the Islamic State group and are among the deadliest in the country's history.

explore_lenses.label: Why does this verdict matter beyond this trial?
explore_lenses.title: Accountability for attackers, not the whole case
explore_lenses.summary: The convictions establish criminal responsibility for people accused of aiding the attacks, but they do not resolve the separate question of why authorities failed to stop them despite warnings or whether others were involved.

claims.text: Sri Lanka’s Supreme Court previously concluded that intelligence warnings indicated churches were vulnerable to imminent attacks, and faulted senior officials for failures to take preventive action.

The Catholic Church welcomed the convictions, while maintaining that those convicted may not represent all of the people responsible for planning the attacks; that broader-conspiracy assertion has not been established in the reporting consulted.

The significance for survivors includes formal judicial recognition after years of proceedings, but unresolved accountability questions concerning security and intelligence failures remain outside this verdict.

The significance for survivors includes formal judicial recognition after years of proceedings, but unresolved accountability questions concerning security and intelligence failures remain outside this verdict.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The verdict does not by itself disclose the court’s full reasoning or determine responsibility of officials who were not defendants in this trial.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach a verdict after seven years?
explore_lenses.title: A large, five-year trial-at-bar
explore_lenses.summary: The prosecution assembled a lengthy case alleging conspiracy and assistance to the suicide bombers, with extensive witness, forensic and physical evidence. The process also faced procedural objections from defense lawyers.

claims.text: The Colombo High Court trial involved 23,270 charges against 24 defendants; prosecutors called 2,309 witnesses and submitted forensic reports and more than 2,000 physical exhibits.
The court ruled that 10 statements made by accused people to police under the Prevention of Terrorism Act could be admitted as evidence.

Defense counsel withdrew in February 2026, according to Human Rights Watch, citing the difficulty of attending daily hearings alongside other cases; four accused then sought a stay, arguing that continuing would violate fair-hearing and presumption-of-innocence rights.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next in the wider investigation?
explore_lenses.title: Sentencing and separate inquiries remain
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate next step is sentencing for the 15 convicted defendants. Separately, investigations concerning alleged conspiracy and possible state-linked responsibility remain active and politically sensitive.

claims.text: Local reporting published after the verdict said nine defendants were acquitted and released, while sentencing of the 15 found guilty was expected shortly.

A separate investigation led to the February 2026 arrest of retired Major General Suresh Sallay on allegations of conspiracy and abetting the attacks; an arrest and allegation are not findings of guilt.

The Archdiocese of Colombo and allied civil-society advocates have called for an independent special prosecutor dedicated to the Easter attacks, arguing that this would improve speed and impartiality; the appointment had not occurred as of April 2026.

story_report.summary: A Sri Lankan court has convicted 15 people over the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, which killed 279 people at three churches and three hotels. The attacks were inspired by the Islamic State group. Reporting after the verdict said nine defendants were acquitted and released, while sentencing for those found guilty was expected shortly. The ruling delivers convictions in one of Sri Lanka’s deadliest attacks, but does not resolve separate questions about security failures or the full scope of responsibility.

sections.heading: Colombo trial evidence and scale
sections.body: The Colombo High Court case covered 23,270 charges against 24 defendants. Prosecutors called 2,309 witnesses and submitted forensic reports along with more than 2,000 physical exhibits. The court also ruled admissible 10 statements that accused people made to police under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. Defense counsel withdrew in February 2026, Human Rights Watch said, citing the difficulty of attending daily hearings alongside other cases; four accused subsequently sought a stay on fair-hearing and presumption-of-innocence grounds.

sections.heading: Accountability questions beyond the defendants
sections.body: Sri Lanka’s Supreme Court had previously found that intelligence warnings indicated churches faced an imminent threat and faulted senior officials for failing to take preventive action. The Catholic Church welcomed the convictions but said those found guilty might not account for everyone who planned the attacks; that broader-conspiracy claim has not been established in the reporting consulted. Separately, retired Major General Suresh Sallay was arrested in February 2026 on allegations of conspiracy and abetting the attacks, though the arrest is not a finding of guilt.

sections.heading: Calls for an independent prosecutor
sections.body: The Archdiocese of Colombo and civil-society advocates have called for an independent special prosecutor focused on the Easter attacks, arguing that such an appointment could improve the speed and impartiality of proceedings. The appointment had not occurred as of April 2026. For survivors, the verdict provides formal judicial recognition after years of proceedings, while accountability questions related to security and intelligence failures remain outside the trial’s immediate outcome.

unresolved.text: The consulted reporting does not establish the sentences for the 15 convicted defendants, the status of any appeals, or how the court addressed each defense objection in its final judgment.
The verdict does not disclose the court’s full reasoning or determine responsibility for officials who were not defendants in this trial.

related_stories.title: Presley Gerber died at age 27
related_stories.summary: Presley Gerber, the 27-year-old son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and entrepreneur Rande Gerber, has died. A family spokesperson confirmed his death, which is currently being investigated as a suspected overdose. Gerber was found unresponsive at a rehabilitation facility in Los Angeles shortly after checking in.

related_stories.title: Investigation Requested into Juror in Lindsay Clancy Case
related_stories.summary: Lindsay Clancy's attorney has filed a motion requesting the court to investigate a juror who was a holdout during her murder trial, which ended in a mistrial. The motion seeks to examine the juror's cellphone use during deliberations and assess the accuracy of his responses on pre-trial questionnaires and during questioning by the judge.

related_stories.title: Typhoon Dujuan Causes Deaths and Destruction in Japan
related_stories.summary: Typhoon Dujuan has resulted in at least four fatalities and 22 injuries in Japan, with reports of six individuals missing. The storm brought record rainfall and violent winds, leading to landslides and significant power outages affecting thousands of homes near Tokyo. As the typhoon moves away, authorities have begun to downgrade heavy rain and landslide warnings.

related_stories.title: UK Doctor Charged in Connection with Rwanda Genocide
related_stories.summary: Dr. Vincent Brown is set to appear in a London court to face charges related to the 1994 Rwanda genocide. This marks the first time the UK has brought charges against an individual in connection with the events of the genocide.
